nodes.text: Picture a pitcher of juice being mixed. The recipe calls for 2 cups of concentrate and 3 cups of water. Those are the two amounts that go in, and they stay two separate amounts: 2 cups of concentrate, 3 cups of water. Now suppose a friend asked you to pass this recipe along, not as a sentence but as one short pairing of numbers. What would that little pairing be telling your friend about how to mix the juice?

nodes.title: Before you mix
nodes.body: You are making juice from a recipe that calls for 2 cups of concentrate and 3 cups of water, both poured into the pitcher. If a friend asked you to describe this recipe with just one short pairing of numbers instead of a whole sentence, what would that pairing be telling them about how to mix it?

nodes.text: 2 Cups Concentrate to 3 Cups Water: A Ratio That Compares Two Quantities

The juice recipe calls for 2 cups of concentrate and 3 cups of water. Taken together, this pairing is a ratio: a ratio compares two quantities measured in the same kind of unit, and here both quantities are amounts of liquid measured in cups. Writing the ratio for this recipe as 2:3 says "for every 2 cups of concentrate there are 3 cups of water." The two numbers are not two separate facts standing on their own; they form one paired comparison, describing the recipe as a single relationship between the concentrate and the water.

Read the recipe's two quantities in the order the ratio is written and they give 2:3 — 2 cups of concentrate written first, 3 cups of water written second. Write the same recipe's pairing the other way and you get 3:2: 3 cups of concentrate with only 2 cups of water. That swapped pairing is not this recipe read in reverse — it calls for more concentrate and less water, so it would make a stronger, more concentrated mixture. The order of the two quantities is part of what the ratio claims: 2:3 for this recipe is not the same as 3:2 for this recipe.

headers: What the pairing demands of the recipe
rows: 2 cups of concentrate written first, 3 cups of water written second: the juice recipe as it is given.
3 cups of concentrate written first with only 2 cups of water written second: a stronger, more concentrated mixture, which is a different recipe, not the same recipe read in reverse.
nodes.caption: The same recipe written both ways: 2:3 and 3:2. Swapping which quantity is written first changes what the ratio claims, so 2:3 for this recipe is not the same as 3:2 for this recipe.

nodes.title: Order Is Part of the Ratio
nodes.body: Take the juice recipe: 2 cups of concentrate and 3 cups of water. Written in that order, the ratio is 2:3 — concentrate first, water second. Now keep the same recipe but write the pairing the other way, 3:2. That reversed order would demand 3 cups of concentrate with only 2 cups of water, a stronger, more concentrated mixture. That is a different recipe, not the same recipe read in reverse. So the order of the two quantities is part of what the ratio claims: 2:3 for this recipe is not the same as 3:2 for this recipe.

nodes.text: Check: Reading a Ratio in Order

nodes.title: Check Your Reading of the Ratio
nodes.body: A recipe writes a ratio as 2:3. Explain what this comparison means. In your explanation, name both quantities and the unit they are measured in, and use the order in which they are written to justify why 2:3 describes the mixture it does rather than a different one. Remember: if the reversed order described the same mixture, you would have no reason to prefer the written order — so account for the order, and do not treat 2:3 and 3:2 as interchangeable.

nodes.prompt: The juice recipe calls for 2 cups of concentrate and 3 cups of water, written as the ratio 2:3. Order the steps below to show how the same two quantities behave when their positions swap, and why 2:3 is not the same as 3:2.

items.label: Write 2 cups concentrate first, then 3 cups water, as the ratio 2:3.
Read 2:3 as 2 cups concentrate for every 3 cups water.
Swap the same quantities to write the ratio 3:2.
Read 3:2 as 3 cups concentrate for every 2 cups water.
Compare: 3:2 gives a stronger, more concentrated mixture than 2:3.

feedback.correct: Yes — the recipe's quantities appear as 2:3, and swapping their positions gives 3:2, which describes a different, more concentrated mixture. The order of the quantities is part of what the ratio claims.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Start by writing the recipe's quantities in the given order as 2:3, then swap the same two quantities to 3:2 and compare what each order describes. Check the order of your steps against how a ratio's meaning changes when its quantities trade places.

nodes.prompt: A recipe mixes 2 cups of concentrate with 3 cups of water. Which statement correctly describes the ratio written as 2:3?

options.text: 2:3 compares 2 cups of concentrate to 3 cups of water, in that written order.
options.explanation: Correct: the ratio reads the two quantities in the order they are written, both measured in cups.

options.text: 2:3 compares 3 cups of water to 2 cups of concentrate.
options.explanation: Reverses the written order, treating the two quantities as interchangeable.

options.text: 2:3 means the same as 3:2 because both quantities are in cups.
options.explanation: Assumes same units make the order irrelevant, so 2:3 and 3:2 are treated as the same.

options.text: 2:3 compares 2 cups concentrate to the 5 total cups of mixture.
options.explanation: Compares a part to the whole instead of comparing the two same-unit quantities.

feedback.correct: Yes. 2:3 reads in written order: 2 cups of concentrate compared with 3 cups of water, both in cups. Reversing it would describe a different, stronger mixture.
feedback.incorrect: The order matters. 2:3 compares 2 cups of concentrate with 3 cups of water in that order; 3:2 would be the reversed, different comparison, not the same thing.

sections.title: Open attention on the juice recipe and make the reader's question concrete: what does '2 cups concentrate and 3 cups water' actually tell you before you mix it?

Build the core understanding: name the pairing as a ratio, state what a ratio compares, and then make the order claim visible by laying the recipe's two quantities out in reading order and in reversed order.
sections.transition: The recipe is on the table as two concrete amounts; this section turns those two amounts into the named idea the objective asks for and uses a laid-out ordering of the quantities to show why their order cannot be swapped.

sections.title: Check whether the learner can use the ratio for the juice recipe and justify its meaning by the order of the two quantities.
sections.transition: The learner has now seen the ratio defined and has reconstructed the ordered pairing on the recipe; this section asks them to read a recipe ratio in its written order and justify the meaning unaided.
